overview: The Tang dynasty is considered China's golden age, marked by cosmopolitan culture, Buddhist flourishing, poetic achievement and international trade. Chang'an became one of the world's largest cities, connected by the Silk Road to Central Asia, India and Persia.

items.text: The Diamond Sutra, the world's oldest dated printed book, produced using woodblock printing.
Gunpowder formula appears in Daoist alchemical texts.
The great poets Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Wei create masterpieces of Chinese verse.
Buddhist cave temples at Dunhuang filled with murals and sculptures.
Porcelain production begins, though it remained rare and precious.
The monk Xuanzang travels to India, returning with Buddhist texts that he translates.
Christianity arrives in Chang'an; a monument records its reception.
Chang'an reaches a population of one million, with foreign merchants, monks and diplomats.
Tea drinking becomes widespread, with the Classic of Tea written by Lu Yu.
Silk Road trade connects China to Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean.
Tang poetry became the standard for later Chinese literature.
Chinatown in English derives from Tang, reflecting the dynasty's historical importance.

fall.text: The An Lushan Rebellion fatally weakened the dynasty; regional military governors gained power, and the last Tang emperor was deposed by Zhu Wen in 907.
